foods.name: White rice
foods.tagline: Two-thirds water, and the water is what sets the limit.
overview: Cooked white rice is mostly water that the grain soaked up in the pot: 68.4 g of every 100 g is water. The rest is starch, 2.69 g of protein, and next to no sodium, potassium or fat.

problems: USDA FoodData Central's public search API (DEMO_KEY) was rate-limited, so composition data was read from the JSON behind each FDC food page (https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/portal-data/external/<id>; the human page is /food-details/<id>/nutrients). Each constituent's compositionSource has both: 'url' (the page) and 'dataUrl' (the exact JSON fetched). All entries are SR Legacy (US national averages, last updated 2019 or earlier), not NZ FOODfiles products.

No supplier SDS (Sigma-Aldrich, Fisher, Merck) could be opened: those sites timed out or returned 403. LD50s therefore come from NLM ChemIDplus (read via Wayback Machine snapshots, because the live page is only a JavaScript shell) and from PubChem/HSDB (read via the PUG-View API; the 'url' fields give the normal PubChem compound page). PubChem/HSDB agrees with ChemIDplus for NaCl, MgCl2, FeSO4, ZnCl2, CuSO4 and ascorbic acid, but has no rat oral value for KCl (only mouse 383 mg/kg and guinea pig 2500 mg/kg) or for water. So the KCl and water numbers rest on ChemIDplus alone.

Water has no measured rat oral median: ChemIDplus reports > 90 mL/kg, treated here as 90,000 mg/kg with 1 mL = 1 g. That is a lower bound, so the water-limited foods (rice, pasta, oats, lentils, chickpeas, baked beans, tofu, quinoa, flour) have a true lethal mass that is higher than shown. It is also an unusual endpoint (water intoxication), and eating water-bound-in-food is not like drinking it. Headline for flour is water at about 53 kg because nothing else gets lower.

Compound hydrate assumptions: magnesium chloride was taken as the anhydrous salt (ChemIDplus record name says so; Mg = 25.5%), ferrous sulfate as the anhydrous salt (Fe = 36.8%), and cupric sulfate as anhydrous (Cu = 39.8%). If those LD50s were actually measured on hydrates, the element doses would be roughly 36-55% lower, which would shave the lethal food mass but not change any attainability class (Mg is the headline only for chia and sesame; iron/copper are never the headline).

Magnesium sulfate (the more 'famous' magnesium salt) has no rat oral LD50 in ChemIDplus or HSDB (only mouse LDLo 5000 mg/kg and subcutaneous values), so magnesium chloride was used instead. Zinc (zinc chloride 350 mg/kg), copper, selenium (sodium selenite 7 mg/kg) and iron appear only when they ranked in a food's lowest four; none is ever the headline.

Swaps and choices within the assigned list: pasta used 'cooked, enriched, without added salt'; oats used 'regular and quick, unenriched, cooked with water, without salt' (generic, not specifically rolled); cornflakes used the only USDA SR entry, 'Ralston Corn Flakes' (fortified, so iron and vitamin C are high); peanuts used 'dry-roasted, with salt'; peanut butter used 'smooth, with salt'; baked beans used 'canned, plain or vegetarian' (USDA's sauce is not specifically tomato, and the other USDA baked-bean entries contain pork or franks); flour used 'all-purpose, unenriched' as the nearest to NZ plain flour; white bread used 'commercially prepared' (US recipe, higher in salt than some NZ loaves); tofu is the raw/as-sold firm entry set with calcium sulfate.

Oxalate (sesame, almonds, chia, quinoa, etc.) was not considered: FDC SR Legacy has no oxalate values and I did not find an authoritative oxalate table to open. Phosphorus, manganese and B vitamins were not given an LD50 lookup because their candidate lethal masses were well above the shown constituents. Selenium and zinc are included only where they ranked in the lowest four.

Every food lands in 'absurd' (5,000 g or more); the nearest to the line is rolled oats porridge at about 7.5 kg (water). Nothing on this list failed the attainability filter and nothing on it has a documented acute-toxicity problem at ordinary amounts when prepared as specified, so 'flagged' is empty. Real, non-LD50 hazards are noted in each food's realWorldCaveat instead: cooked rice left at room temperature (Bacillus cereus), raw flour (E. coli), dry chia swelling in the oesophagus, nut/peanut/sesame/soy allergy, popcorn choking, cashew shell oil, and the sweet-vs-bitter almond distinction. You may want to flag chia and white-flour on the site if you want a stricter reading of the spec.

Serving-unit gram weights come from each FDC entry's food measures (SR Legacy household measures), except '1 kg' which is a definition. I did not use brand pack sizes because I could not source them. Fun facts are general-knowledge, deliberately contain no dates or numbers, and were not URL-checked; treat them as 'worth a skim'. The numbers inside some fun facts (e.g., peanut butter fat, tofu calcium) are the USDA values from this file.
